title: No openings for Black jazz leaders
summary: Hall compares Ruby Braff and Scott Hamilton with Black players, and asks how much Miles and Coltrane worked.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: But there just haven't been any openings for the Black Jazz musician. You go to a club, you got to bargain for scale, and that reduces the type of guys you're going to have to have with you, because it's not enough money. But you get a Ruby Braff can go and demand and get whatever he wants, or even Scott Hamilton AND HE'S NEW.
Well, I know in the case of Ruby, though, he went many years where he was, you know, not in vogue or in favor, and he didn't work that much either.
When he worked, he made it.
Well, then he went with Tony Bennett. That's how he survived, you know. That was a good paying gig. But that wasn't a jazz job, you know.
Yeah, but that wasn't because of his playing.
Scott Hamilton just happened to come along in a period when jazz has become more popular again and --
He's a beautiful player, though. Don't get me wrong. He sounds nice, his whole band. But they haven't got any leaders that could get a job out of any of these bands, a Black person put in charge.
Well, some players did come out of, you know, talking -- going back to that era -- come out of the Charlie Parker, Dizzy Gillespie, you know, period, who did go on to become like Miles Davis.
They weren't making any money.
Well, Miles did pretty well for himself.
Afterwards.
Yeah,
That's much later. We're talking about coming up into the -- into the foundation of all of this.
Well, then there were only a few leaders, you know, and everyone else was a side man. It wasn't until the '50s that a lot of these musicians became, you know, leaders.
Well, most of them were leaders only because they were able to get double fee for the job, and they got the job.

No, but I mean out of that -- out of those bands came some people that became personalities who then formed their own groups like, you know, Coltrane and Miles, you know, Miles, and then Coltrane played with Miles, and then he got a reputation, and he had his own group, you know. That's the way that seems to have develop. But it just seemed --
But how many weeks did they work and where? You're speaking about a lifetime of playing.
Yeah.
Not an engagement here or there, because it wasn't acceptable all over the country; for if it Coltrane wasn't at the Village Vanguard...
Yeah, there were certain clubs in certain big cities.
